txt: ... though what, exactly, you can't say. He turns the rifle over again, admiring the glint of light off the oily barrel.
A moment of silence. They're waiting for you to speak.
Another sigh. “It's an unfortunate story. You see, our ex-comrade Maurice is something of an economist...”
He nods to your shirt. "No offence, of course."
He sighs. "Right, then there was the whole 'turnip' debacle."
He sighs. "That's Cindy's stuff. She just sort of... moved it all in a few months ago."
He sighs. "There's more to it than that. People still make their own choices. It's a matter of being aware what's influencing them."
He sighs. "Yeah, it's hers. She just sort of... moved it all in a few months ago."
He sighs. "You're right. It probably wouldn't *kill* us to read more conventional historical materialism."
He turns to his companion. "Can you imagine the look on Maurice's face when he finds out the RCM has been kicking my door down?"
The two young men are either oblivious to or ignoring your entrance. Their attentions are fixed on whatever it is they're stacking in the middle of the floor...
The young man appears lost inside his own thoughts...
The young man can hardly conceal his disappointment. He was apparently looking forward to being punched by you.
The young man considers your words for a minute.
The young man frowns at the little pile of boxes on the floor.
The young man gives his companion an uncertain glance. The companion nods his head vigorously.
The young man gives you a concerned look.
The young man gives you a slightly confused look, as though he's sure you asked something else and he simply misheard.
The young man grimaces. It seems he's less than 100% comfortable with war crimes.
The young man ignores the lieutenant. "But I suppose it makes sense that some common strain of infra-materialist thought would persist in the RCM, even to this day, given its origins."
The young man looks at you a moment, then at his companion.
The young man nods but says nothing. He appears to be distracted by something...
The young man nods thoughtfully. "But I suppose it makes sense that some common strain of infra-materialist thought would persist in the RCM, even to this day, given its origins."
The young man pushes back his shirt sleeves, revealing the pale flesh of his forearms.
The young man raises his fist in reply and gives you a curt nod.
The young man sighs. His companion looks about furtively.
The young man sighs. "God, it's so pitiful watching a grown man beg. I can hardly stand it."
The young man staggers back into the couch, eyes agog and momentarily dazed, but not seriously hurt.
The young man takes the folded up magazine with some hesitation. As he reads over your annotations and emendations a look of deep concentration comes over his face...
The young man waits patiently for you to finish.
When he's finished, he returns the rifle to you with a nod of appreciation.
"'Confiscated'? Next he's probably going to say it was civil asset forfeiture..."
"'In dark times, should the stars also go out?'"
"'Some other way'?" He squints at you. "If you're not much of a reader, why are you so dead-set on joining this reading group?"
"'The deal'? At a fundamental level I guess you could call it the shattered bones of a dream crushed by capital."
"*Or* it suggests that capital, in sufficient quantities, must exhibit its own plasm-like qualities..."
"*Sorry*? You nearly took my fucking jaw off!"
"*You've* read our article?" For the first time since you've met the young man, words seem to desert him...
"... I'm just saying it's *heavily implied* that welkin are the bourgeoisie of the Wirrâl setting..."
"... I'm just trying to imagine what it would have been like had he died in the summer..."
"... and next thing you know there are *budget cuts*, so now we've got to cut the bean rations in half *again*..."
"... and there it goes..."
"... and we still don't know what happened to the rest of his armour..."
"... assuming he's even still interested, that is."
"... but I still don't see what the lady driver had to do with the strike stand-off..."
"... but don't you think that pornographic fascist mythology gets pretty tiresome after a few books?"
"... but if it's true that this individual possesses *so much capital* that light literally *bends* around him, then that must mean..."
"... but my question is where does the RCM *recruit* all these hyper-revolutionaries to join this 'Remote Viewers Division'?"
"... but then my issue with these historical cube-pushers is that they offer the *illusion* of subjectivity even as they reinscribe the logic of colonialism itself..."
"... but then, any *critical* account of Dolores Dei's reign has to seriously reckon with her atrocities in Magritania and La Vuelta during the Mesque secession, don't you think?"
"... but to Comrade Ulixes' point, isn't there value in reading really difficult books, just for the sheer challenge of it?"
"... so is it typical for men of your background to use that, um, formulation?"
"... though I'd love to hear your take on it."
"A Gottwaldian would tell you that it's an inescapable fact of modernity that we can only repackage our collective history in increasingly ludicrous forms..."  He nods.
"A compelling point, for sure. We'd probably be better off if more police officers learned to think so reflectively about their social function."

"A fair point. It also reminds me of one of Mazov and Nilsen's unrealized projects, a universal system of communist pictographs, one that would allow revolutionaries to communicate and organise across any language barrier."
"A story with an erotico-political angle. Let's see where this goes..."
"A thought can be a very powerful thing. That's the whole idea of infra-materialism..."
"Aaagh! Shit!"
"About that question you asked earlier. It reminded me of a certain poem that you might appreciate..."
"Absolutely not. You have to keep it..."
"Absolutely. It's the only proper foundation to develop a real understanding of events." He nods in vigorous agreement.
"Ah, I see. That's certainly kind of you." He gives you a curious half-smile.
"Ah, gendarme. Your problem isn't ideological, it's personal..."
"Ah, it makes sense. There's already a sub-theme of radical street art running through our reading group..."
"Ah, right. You were playing the long game."
"Ah, so there *is* a supra-natural angle to this case..."
"Ah, well there's certainly value in that kind of reading. Comrade Mazov says something on that note in his collected speeches..."
"Ah, yes. That's certainly one of the *least* developed parts of the theory, but also one of the most intriguing."
"Aha, a real old-school pedestrian materialist. Alright, we'll play along..."
"Alright, gendarme, your turn."
"Alright, gendarme." He turns back to you. "Comrade Ulixes and I have conferred about it, and we've come up with an alternative way for you to convince us of your commitment to the group."
"Alternatively, it could be that our own ideological fervour is still *insufficient*."
"An interesting point, Uli."
"And Graadian realism is the worst realism. It's nearly as bad as Gottwaldian critical theory."
"And I don't think she could afford rent at an actual studio."
"And before that we spent six weeks on 'State and Plasm'..."
"And now they've sent one of their agents to *infiltrate* our meeting." He rubs his hands together excitedly.
"And now they've shown up *in force* to break up our meeting!" He rubs his hands together excitedly.
"And with that, welcome to the most ideologically advanced materialist reading group in Martinaise!"
"Anyway, goodnight to you."

"Anyway, we also enjoy a good board game every once in a while. The other week Ulixes and I tried this new one where everyone is competing to manage their own Zone of Ecological Catastrophe. You should see the components."
"Are you absolutely sure? A communist can't be afraid to ask questions, just because they don't know what the answer might be."
"Are you saying you *haven't* done the reading for tonight?"  The two young men look at one another.
"Basically, he was rejecting the whole foundation of infra-materialist theory."
"Because I always have. Though I try not to do it too often now... it's kind of embarrassing, isn't it?"
"Besides, it's inconceivable that we'd turn down a fellow Wirrâl enthusiast..."
"Besides, it's just a first draft."
"But at least crime literature *as a genre* is able to engage with the systemic failures of capitalism."
"But given that we have some extra seating at the moment, I guess we could be convinced to expedite an application or two."
"But how did you... oh, never mind. I guess I'm easier to read than I thought..."
"But it's getting late, so maybe pick the *most important* question?"
"But more specifically, we're running a reading group, the most rigorous and theoretically advanced materialist reading group in Martinaise."
"But no matter. What's on your mind?"
"But now we're getting hung up on the pathologies of capitalism. Let's move on."
"But seriously, the next campaign, you've got to be there. I need to see this hybrid in action."
"But to be perfectly frank, I just don't see it happening."
"But, of course, our *special emphasis* is on the theories of Ignus Nilsen and his followers, especially the infra-materialists."
"Can I hold it?"
"Careful, careful!"
"Characters? What characters are you talking about?"
"Cindy is... how to describe her *role*..."
"Clearly there's a lot of ins-and-outs. It almost reminds me of a Dick Mullen novel."
"Cockatoos? Fascinating. So tell us what you gathered from your ornithological researches."
"Combining the best race with the worst race... Not sure about the skill progressions, but I bet the role-playing opportunities are *wild*."
"Come back when you're done." He gives you a brief nod as he hands you the slim guide. "We'll be here pretty much every night after 22.00."
"Come on, gendarme. Real progress requires great risks."
"Come on. It's not that I don't *have* anything to say about Cindy's art. It's more that I'm... still working out the details. It's a complex question, you've got to take your time with it..."
"Come on. We have things to do in the morning."
"Comrade Ulixes is right. The amount of plasm required to strike down an ideological enemy outright is enormous. We're talking second-level effects, at a minimum."
"Damn. Hardly any difference..." The young man shakes his head, and then looks up at you with barely concealed irritation...
"Do be sure to take your time with the reading. We'll be eager to hear your thoughts."
"Do you know the story of Dobreva and Abadanaiz?"
"Do you think all the problems in the world can be reduced to repressed sexual urges?"
"Don't apologise. As I was saying, if it were *easy*, it wouldn't require so much plasm to work."
"Easy, Uli..."
"Either way, that's enough parlour games for one night. Thanks for humouring us."
"Errrrck." The young man cradles his jaw and looks up, his expression blank.
"Especially then."
"Even then."
"Everything alright, gendarme? You look a little green about the gills..."
"Everything, man. That is part of the communist project, to destroy the ideological structures that reduce men and women to these hollow shells of identity."
"Exactly! I was thinking we could print them in the old communard style, with huge slogans..."
"Exactly. The only worthwhile part of the so-called École normale de Revachol is the library. That's where we've made our greatest critical strides."
"Exactly. What educated person could believe that turnips grow at the same rate under capitalism *and* communism?"
"Fascinating..."
"For a second there I thought we had it. Just goes to show how constrained we are under the limits of the prevailing regime."
"For starters, they love talking about *beans*."
"For us the question boiled down to: 'If you don't even accept the basic ideas of Nilsen and infra-materialist theory, why are you in the reading group?'"
"Glad to hear it. I was thinking we might be able to get Cindy to design the posters..."
"Go ahead and take a seat. Since we haven't had time to prepare an exhaustive questionnaire, I think we can keep this interview more freeform."
"Go ahead." The young man gives you a half-smile. His companion sniffs.
"Good god, have we really been talking about the alphabet for a quarter hour?"  He looks down at his watch.
"Good point, Uli."
"Good point. So as a provisional matter, I can say we support it."
"Grain spirits are dangerous. That's why Comrade Mazov himself preferred chamomile tea, as I'm sure you're aware."
"Ha! It's good you were able to see through even that gauzy nostalgic pulp."
"Ha! Of course you do. I just hope when you're reading it you've got a sturdy pair of gloves on..."

"He *also* happens to be the greatest communist theorist after Mazov himself. It was Nilsen who first postulated the existence of ideological plasm, which forms the basis of infra-materialist theory."
"Here's your first assignment. It's an overview of infra-materialist theory. A little basic, as you'll see, but one has to start somewhere."
"Hmm, don't think I'm familiar with it. Give us a quick summary, if you don't mind."
"Hmm, so you're saying you've got to have a certain practical foundation before you move onto more abstract topics. Okay, I'm following..."
"Hmmm, I guess you could call her latest stuff a sort of *counter-bourgeois calligraphy*. She's got a real taste for radical slogans."
"Hmmm. I thought I perceived some *eschatological* air about you..."
"I am serious. As materialists we've got to adapt to conditions as they are. Besides, he'll still need to pass the *interview portion* of the entrance process..." He turns back to you.
"I assumed it was Maurice who broke into my room, to play a trick on me. I didn't think I'd *actually* been raided by the RCM!"
"I can tell you're a man who has his urges, but I can also tell you're no Gottwaldian." He smirks.
"I do have to admire a certain tenacity, even when it seems to make no sense."
"I do hope they revise it in the next edition. But for now, I'm quite proud of the high welkin I built for our most recent campaign."
"I don't think so."  The young man gives you a curious look. "Unless you've been hanging around the Cultural Studies faculty at the École Normale de Revachol..."

"I guess you could say we believe it *because it's impossible*." He looks at the scattered matchboxes on the ground. "It's our way of saying we refuse to accept that the world has to remain... like this..."
"I have to say, I never realised humans and cockatoos had so much in common."
"I have to say, I've never *entirely* understood what they mean, but I think maybe the answer is in there, somewhere."
"I suppose that would open us up to charges of hypocrisy... not to mention it might make us *look pretty desperate* for new members..."
"I suppose we are all here to advance our studies in some form or another..."

"I suppose we'll have to leave it there. But listen, gendarme: We could use someone with your *breadth of expertise*. With just a little more theoretical background, I think you'll be able to make some real contributions."
"I think it's holding, Ulixes..."
"I think she'll get there, though. She's still looking for a subject equal to her ambitions."
"I thought so, too, but perhaps we overdid it, just a little..."
"I want us *all* to live in a better world. But yes... she's a part of it... I guess we're all a part of it..."
"I want you... to hit me."
"I'll grant you it can be overwhelming at first, but once you understand the basics, it's all quite intuitive..."
"I'll say that beginnings are very delicate things. That makes it all the more important that you start with *the right books*."
"I'm fine. Better than fine, actually." The young man rubs his cheek. "Perhaps we should tangle with the gendarmerie more often."
"I'm just trying to imagine what it would be like to wake up with no concept of what money is..."
"I'm not saying we abandon our beliefs. I just think it would be better if our group had more than *two* regular attendees."
"I'm not sure I get what you're driving at. Of course there will be a future, even if the form it takes might appear unrecognisable. That's the spiral of progress."
"I'm not sure it would do very much good. She's sort of... impervious to authority."
"I'm sure as a gendarme you have a *very* interesting take on the Mullen character."
"I've been thinking about what you asked before, about women, you know..."
"If infra-materialism is wrong, I don't want to be right."
"If it were, they wouldn't keep committing suicide."
"In any case, I think we've heard enough. We could use someone with your perspective in the group. With just a bit more theoretical foundation, I think you'll be making real contributions."
"In any case, I'm glad our piece found its audience. That's always the hope with these things, you know."
"In any case, we've kept you long enough. Goodnight to you."
"In the most general sense, I would say we're cultivating revolutionary consciousness."

"Intellectual attrition is maybe the best way to describe it. Felix said he couldn't keep up with the reading on top of his classwork. And Zuzanna wanted to read texts *other than* Mazovian theory. Like novels, if you can believe it..."
"Interesting, I always thought that stuff was common folk superstitions repackaged as bourgeois spiritualism, but maybe I've been overly dismissive?"
"Interesting. Does that mean you've done the reading?"
"Interesting. Say more about that..."
"Interesting. So you're saying that in a certain sense the *game plays the players* as much as they play the game?"
"Is everything alright? Is there something you're trying to say?"
"Is it... it's holding... it's holding!"
"It *is* miserable. That's probably why they're always committing suicide."
"It certainly *looks* like my jacket, Ulixes. Where did you get that, gendarme?"
"It makes sense, though. Mazovianism stresses the essential continuity between humanity and nature, so anything you find in one should be reflected in the other. What's the exact quote, Uli?"
"It seems like there's something on your mind. Maybe a question you mean to ask?"  The young man turns to his companion, then back to you.
"It seems you're right, Uli. I should've listened to you." He sighs, then turns to you.

"It was written by a young communard who was killed on the barricades during the Coalition landings. The story goes that he wrote it on the last night of his life, keeping watch from the barricades in the middle of the night. I don't have the whole thing committed to memory, but there's a line in it I think about sometimes."
"It's a symptom, in other words. Not a cause." He waves his hand as though this is all there is to say on the subject of crime.
"It's a world-historical nightmare," the young man says gravely. "One from which we've yet to awaken."
"It's an old construction site." He looks around. "They've been trying to restore these apartments for years, but as you can see they haven't made much progress."
"It's fine, Uli. That's enough parlour games for one night. We should clean up."

"It's from them we get the notion of dual-leadership, the *décomptage*, Revachol's truly great contribution to revolutionary thought. I believe it even persists in some form in the RCM, even to this day."
"It's heavier than I was expecting." The rifle rests in his open palms. Its position reminds you of something...
"It's no wonder you couldn't finish it. Sounds like turgid bourgeois social realism." He nods approvingly.

"It's nothing like that. A yank-fest is a decadent bourgeois phenomenon, a pastime for over-educated office workers who lack proper revolutionary outlets for their social dissatisfactions and repressed sexuality."
"It's okay for Uli to say that because his dad is from Gottwald."
"It's pretty awesome, I won't deny it."
"It's really nothing like that." The young man scoffs. "A book club is a place for talking about the plot points of bourgeois social novels and sipping effervescent cocktails."
"It's so good. Brutally revelatory."
"It's sweet how excited you are. Come back when you're done. We'll be here pretty much every night after 22.00."
"Julia Dobreva came from Graad. Jean Abadanaiz was born in Revachol. She was brilliant, charismatic, a revolutionary comet. He was her partner and stabiliser, the planet who kept her in orbit."
"Kind of chilly tonight, Uli."
"Listen, this is a forward-thinking group. It's entirely your business, of course."
"Lynching? No. We're not an *operational* cell."
"Makes sense. Based on my experience, you've got to let her see that you've grown, ideologically speaking..."
"Makes sense. It doesn't seem like there's anywhere else she could have gone."
"Makes sense. It's natural to seek out reflections of your own experience in literature when the politico-economic system doesn't permit genuine self-realization."
"Maurice and Zuzanna will be back, I know it."
"Maybe it's a question of degree."
"Maybe your problem is that you think it's their job to *handle* you..."
"Maybe your problem is that you think they're *yours* to handle..."
"Mmm, yeah that's not bad."
"Mmmm." The young man considers you a moment...
"More what?"
"My god, is it really holding?"
"My grades are trash this semester."
"My mums." The young man looks surprised. "She works in one of those skyscrapers, but it's not like you think... she's a cleaning lady..."
"Nilsen. Ignus Nilsen."
"No, it's just like Mazov wrote: 'The freeman of the future will be he who awakens in perfect ignorance of Capital'."
"No, keep it. I feel... *great*, actually..." He turns to his companion. "Perhaps we should tangle with the gendarmerie more often."
"No, unfortunately. The communards were hunted down and killed nearly to a man. All that's left of them are bones and old rifles."
"No, we're an independent organisation," he says proudly. "We acknowledge and respect the Union's efforts, but our interests are more theoretical than Mr. Claire's."
"No-no-no. We're saying he doesn't *need* to open them, because he absorbs all the relevant content just by staring intently at the cover. It's a widely understood second-level effect..."
"No. They were the Revolutionary Lovers, the Dual Commissars of Revolution in Insulinde."
"No." He looks up. "It was exactly what's *supposed* to happen. We should treat it that way."
"Nobody said fulfilling the proletariat's historic role would be easy." A tight smile. "It demands great faith with no promise of tangible reward. But that doesn't mean we can simply give up."
"Not exactly the second incarnation of Kras Mazov, is he?" The young man considers the figurine with a slight grimace.
"Not just lovers, they were the Dual Commissars of Revolution in Insulinde."
"Not that it's any of my business, but it sounds like this question is *really* tearing you up inside."
"Nothing *too major*, I think. We were talking, potentially, about relaxing some parts of our admissions process..."
"Nothing, just messing around until the meeting started."
"Now, if you'll excuse us, we have some *group business* to attend to."
"Of course it's possible. Just extremely difficult. You practically have to be a world-historical individual to do it."
"Of course not. The only people who actually call themselves liberals are mouth-foaming reactionaries."
"Of course you do. It's pretty basic stuff!"
"Of course. The one thing capitalism does better than every other ideology is novel and clever distractions. It's all one never-ending dopamine dripper."
"Of course. What would I even do with it?" He gives you a half-smile.
"Oh! And, gendarme. One last thing..."
"Oh, I *like* that. We're dismantling the structures of capital with their own tools..."
"Oh, gendarme, because this is perfect..."
"Oh, it *is*, and it only gets *more disco* from here..."
"Oh, it's a great story. You should check out Nilsen's journals if you ever have the chance."
"Oh, please. There's nothing 'moderate' about their love for counting beans. If I were a Gottwaldian, I would probably diagnose them with *Bohnenfixierung*..."
"Oh, right. 'Sixteen Days of Coldest... Whatever'. What was your take on it?"
"Oh, right. We've been meaning to try that out."
"Oh, sure, we don't mean to deny the value of *pleasure* in reading."

"Oh, sure. But Econoclards are *obsessed* with beans. They love thinking about beans, they love counting beans, but most of all, they love building models to predict how many beans there'll be *in the future*."
"Oh, sure. But you can always join a *book club* if that's what you're into."
"Oh, sure. It's definitely *interesting*, I would say..."
"Oh, we're getting into the psychiatric pathologies of life under capital. Let's see where this goes..."
"Oh, yes. Or the *fun parts*, as we like to call them."
"Oh, you want to start *now*?" He looks to his companion, then back at you. "Sure, we can manage that..."
"Oh? Sounds nice, actually. Comrade Mazov himself preferred chamomile tea, as I'm sure you're aware."
"Okay, we'll bite." The young man and his companion look at one another, then turn back to you. "What sort of stories are we talking about?"
"One of capitalism's more banal pathologies. But let's move on."
"One thing you learn quickly at university is that you're not going to find a real education in any lecture hall or discussion seminar."
"Only Kras Mazov's most trusted lieutenant, the Evangelist of the Revolution, and the founding father of the People's Republic of Samara."

"Only in this very specific sense. Communism doesn't dangle any promises of eternal bliss or reward. The only promise it offers is that the future can be better than the past, if we're willing to work and fight and die for it."
"Our stance? What, does he want to know if the SRV has established a party line on lynchings in Martinaise?" The two young men look at one another.
"Perhaps some vestigial sexual objectification from your pre-revolutionary consciousness." He nods.
"Plus, I've got the *perfect* place in mind..."
"Plus, all these empty chairs are a little sad, aren't they?"
"Puncher and Wattmann should be required reading."
"Put some more coffee on, Uli. We've got a long night ahead of us. We should probably get Cindy in here too..."
"Right, of course it is." He gives you a sad half-smile.
"Right. Basically an infra-materialist parlour game. Let's forget about it."
"Right. Sure he does." He gives you a sly half-smile.
"Right. We'll have to table this question until we've considered the potential downstream effects."
"See, Uli? It's just like Mazov wrote. How does it go again?"
"See? You're already falling for that scarcity logic. You start off *assuming* there aren't enough beans to go around, so naturally you want to cut the bean rations in half..."
"Shhh. This is the most amazing thing I've ever seen..."
"Simply that *under suitably revolutionary conditions* crop yields naturally increase relative to non-revolutionary crops. Which Maurice somehow has the gall to deny."
"So have you figured out his real identity?"
"So what sort of practical works are we talking about?"
"So you really *did* read all the way to the end." A sheepish grin. "Yeah, Uli and I were trying to see whether there was enough plasm between the two of us to hold up a few matchboxes..."
"So you're saying it didn't suck to interrogate her later? I find that unlikely..."
"So, good luck with that, I guess."
"Something else..." The young man shakes his head.
"Sounds like old-fashioned revolutionary espionage. Let's see where this goes..."
"Sounds to me like a typical bourgeois social novel, designed to assuage the egos of frustrated housewives and win international awards."
"Sure, right. I got the main idea anyway."
"Sure, we're here most every night." He shrugs. "Maybe we'll catch you again."
"Thanks, I appreciate it."
"Thanks, Uli. When the idea is sound the words just sort of flow."
"That could be." He nods. "It would explain some of the more ornate detailing. But we're speaking in world-historical terms here. What this place *represents*, not what it merely *was*."
"That doesn't stop her from using the room for studio space, of course."
"That girl from my seminar *promised* she would stop by."
"That's *exactly* what I was thinking..."
"That's a fair point. Personally, I've never understood the point of picking a human in the Wirrâl setting, but to each their own."
"That's a fascinating trajectory, for sure. It's good to hear that you can still grow ideologically even at an... um... advanced age."
"That's an unfortunate quality of pulp fiction. Much of it is written to be disposable both on an intellectual *and* a material level."
"That's because your brain is floating in ideology, gendarme. It's practically drowning in it..."
"That's easy: Crime is simply the inevitable expression of the injustice and incoherence embedded within capitalism itself."
"That's enough, Uli. It's the gendarme's opinions we're interested in."
"That's our whole *thing*. The world is so shallow, all noise and repetition. We're interested in genuinely radical critique."

"That's right. Econoclards are *obsessed* with beans. They love thinking about beans, they love counting beans, but most of all, they love building models to predict how many beans there'll be *in the future*."
"That's the whole point, of course. We can't just have *anybody* waltzing in here. Martinaise is crawling with reactionary infiltrators."
"That's true. I recall from one of psycholinguistics lectures that the letter 'A' is derived from the proto-Perikarnassian glyph meant to represent a reed hut."
"That's what ideology is. It's like there are these invisible forces everywhere, pushing and tugging you this way and that, and you don't even know they're *there*."
"That's why they spend all their time smoking cigarettes and writing long works of criticism that make you want to commit suicide."
"That... was *amazing*. Uli, perhaps we should tangle with the gendarmerie more often." The young man rubs his cheek.
"The Gottwald School believe that intellectuals as a class are incapable of sparking revolutionary change, so all they can do is *critique* capitalism from inside itself."
"The Insulindian Deluge wiped out an entire generation of communists. Afterward, they were all bulldozed into mass graves." The young man looks slightly queasy at the thought.
"The RCM wants to join us?" A quizzical expression...
"The gendarme returns." The young man turns to you. "What do you need?"
"The only 'class' I care about is the working class."
"The original Fizdale translation, not that watered-down revisionist garbage."
"The so-called 'Revolutionary Lovers'. They were the Dual Commissars of Revolution in Insulinde."

"The theorists Puncher and Wattmann -- not infra-materialists, but theorists nonetheless -- say that communism is a secular version of Perikarnassian theology, that it replaces faith in the divine with faith in humanity's future..."
"The two phenomena are actually deeply intertwined." He nods. "Many infra-materialists believe that pale is actually a manifestation of nostalgia and historical inertia..."
"The whole innocentic system practically requires that. Without true gods we're made to set them up for ourselves." He nods vigorously.
"Then you don't believe in the historic role of the proletariat, which also means you reject the basis of historical materialism."
"Theory is the poetry of thought."
